newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's BOE slams restrictive monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's BOE slams restrictive monetary policy.

text.p: The Board of Executors on Wednesday slammed the South African Reserve Bank's "unjustifiably restrictive" monetary policy and called for an immediate cut in the Bank rate.
"The main obtsacle to the achievement of higher growth rates is now an unjustifiably restrictive monetary policy," BOE economist Rob Lee said in his latest Investment Outlook.
"The Bank rate should have already been cut and further delay seems inexcusable."
Bank rate, the official lending rate which was last hiked by one percentage point in November last year, currently stands at 17 percent.

Lee, who has repeatedly warned in recent months that the economy was in danger of going into recession, said that even if that was technically averted, 1997 and 1998 would be years of weak economic growth.
"These views have now become widespread," Lee said.

South Africa already came in at the bottom of the league in growth forecasts for emerging markets at 1.5 percent for 1997 and 2.5 percent for 1998, while its real prime lending rate was the highest among a group of both developed and developing countries at 11.5 percent.

It was therefore not surprising that South Africa had attracted little foreign investment and that most emerging market portfolio investors were substantially underweight in the South African share market.
"Recent capital inflows have been predominantly into South African bonds as foreign investors perceive that interest rates are far too high and must eventually fall sharply," Lee said.

South Africa's inflation rate was generally expected to fall significantly next year, possibly by three percent from current levels, while inflation in most other countries was expected to be stable or to even rise slightly.
"South Africa's real rates based on prospective inflation are therefore absurdly out of line," Lee said.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said told state radio earlier on Wednesday that he was hopeful of an interest rate cut by the end of the year in the wake of recent encouraging inflation, money supply and trade data.
